Questions.Title: Question 1
Questions.QuestionText: A manufacturing process produces electronic components with a defect rate of 5%. If you randomly select 3 components what is the probability that exactly 2 of them are defective?
Questions.Feedback: This is a binomial probability problem. With n = 3 components k = 2 defective components and p = 0.05 probability of defect we calculate

Questions.Title: Question 2
Questions.QuestionText: An electrical engineer tests a batch of 100 resistors and finds that 8 are outside the acceptable tolerance range. If three resistors are randomly selected for a circuit what is the probability that at least one will be outside the acceptable tolerance range?
Questions.Feedback: The probability of selecting a resistor outside tolerance is 8/100 = 0.08. The probability that all three are within tolerance is 0.92^3 = 0.7787. Therefore the probability that at least one is outside tolerance is 1 - 0.7787 = 0.2213 (rounded to 0.221).

Questions.Title: Question 3
Questions.QuestionText: A civil engineer is analyzing the reliability of a bridge design. The probability of the bridge failing under extreme weather conditions is 0.001. If five similar bridges are built in a region prone to extreme weather what is the probability that at least one bridge will fail during such conditions over their lifetime?
Questions.Feedback: The probability of a single bridge not failing is 0.999. For five independent bridges the probability that none fail is 0.999^5 = 0.995. Therefore the probability that at least one fails is 1 - 0.995 = 0.005.

Questions.Title: Question 4
Questions.QuestionText: A chemical engineer designs a batch reactor where three independent safety systems are installed. Each system has a reliability of 0.95 (probability of working when needed). What is the probability that at least one safety system will operate during an emergency?
Questions.Feedback: The probability of one system failing is 0.05. For all three systems to fail we calculate 0.05^3 = 0.000125. The probability that at least one works is 1 - 0.000125 = 0.999875.

Questions.Title: Question 5
Questions.QuestionText: A mechanical engineer is designing a system with two parallel pumps. Each pump has a 0.2 probability of failing during operation. The system continues to function if at least one pump works. What is the probability that the system will function properly?
Questions.Feedback: In a parallel system failure occurs only when all components fail. The probability of both pumps failing is 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04. Therefore

Questions.Title: Question 6
Questions.QuestionText: An aerospace engineer is testing a new material for aircraft components. Historical data shows that 30% of similar materials fail stress tests. If 4 samples of the new material are tested independently what is the probability that exactly 2 will pass the stress test?
Questions.Feedback: Since 30% fail 70% pass. Using the binomial formula with n = 4 k = 2 and p = 0.7

Questions.Title: Question 7
Questions.QuestionText: A software engineer finds that 15% of all user requests to a server result in errors. If 20 independent requests are made what is the probability that fewer than 3 requests will result in errors?
Questions.Feedback: We need P(X < 3) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + P(X = 2) where X is the number of errors in 20 requests with p = 0.15.

Questions.Title: Question 8
Questions.QuestionText: An industrial engineer is analyzing a manufacturing system with two sequential processes. Process A has a 90% yield rate and Process B has an 85% yield rate. What is the probability that a randomly selected unit will successfully pass through both processes?
Questions.Feedback: For a unit to pass through both processes it must pass Process A (0.90 probability) AND Process B (0.85 probability). Using the multiplication rule for independent events

Questions.Title: Question 9
Questions.QuestionText: A telecommunications engineer designs a network where data packets have a 2% chance of being corrupted during transmission. If 10 packets are sent independently what is the probability that exactly 9 packets will arrive uncorrupted?
Questions.Feedback: With n = 10 packets k = 9 uncorrupted packets p = 0.98 probability of uncorrupted transmission

Questions.Title: Question 10
Questions.QuestionText: A structural engineer is analyzing the failure modes of a building during an earthquake. There are three critical structural components each with an independent 0.1 probability of failing during a severe earthquake. What is the probability that exactly one of these components will fail?
Questions.Feedback: Using the binomial formula with n = 3 k = 1 and p = 0.1

Questions.Title: Question 11
Questions.QuestionText: The probability of any event must always be:
Questions.Feedback: By the axioms of probability, the probability of any event must be between 0 and 1 inclusive, where 0 means impossible and 1 means certain

Questions.Title: Question 12
Questions.QuestionText: What is the sample space of a random experiment?
Questions.Feedback: The sample space, often denoted by Ω or S, is the set of all possible outcomes that can result from a random experiment

Options.Text: The set of possible outcomes we're interested in
The set of all possible outcomes of the experiment
The set of outcomes with equal probabilities
The set of most likely outcomes

Questions.Title: Question 13
Questions.QuestionText: The probability of the entire sample space S is always:
Questions.Feedback: The sample space contains all possible outcomes, so something from the sample space must occur with certainty. Therefore P(S) = 1

Questions.Title: Question 14
Questions.QuestionText: The probability of an impossible event is:
Questions.Feedback: An impossible event (often denoted by ∅, the empty set) has a probability of 0, representing that it will never occur

Questions.Title: Question 15
Questions.QuestionText: If P(A) = 0.35, what is P(A')?
Questions.Feedback: For any event A, P(A) + P(A') = 1. So P(A') = 1 - P(A) = 1 - 0.35 = 0.65

Options.Text: Cannot be determined without more information

Questions.Title: Question 16
Questions.QuestionText: Two events A and B are mutually exclusive if:
Questions.Feedback: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously, meaning A ∩ B = ∅ (the empty set) and P(A ∩ B) = 0

Questions.Title: Question 17
Questions.QuestionText: If events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A ∪ B)?
Questions.Feedback: For mutually exclusive events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8

Questions.Title: Question 18
Questions.QuestionText: For any two events A and B, which formula correctly gives P(A ∪ B)?
Questions.Feedback: The general addition rule is P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B) to avoid counting the intersection twice

Questions.Title: Question 19
Questions.QuestionText: Two events A and B are independent if:
Questions.Feedback: Events are independent if the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other, mathematically expressed as P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)

Questions.Title: Question 20
Questions.QuestionText: If events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.25, what is P(A ∩ B)?
Questions.Feedback: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.1

Questions.Title: Question 21
Questions.QuestionText: The conditional probability P(A|B) represents:
Questions.Feedback: P(A|B) represents the probability of event A occurring given that event B has already occurred

Options.Text: The probability of A or B occurring
The probability of A and B both occurring
The probability of A not occurring given B occurs
The probability of A occurring given that B has occurred

Questions.Title: Question 22
Questions.QuestionText: If P(A ∩ B) = 0.15 and P(B) = 0.3, what is P(A|B)?

Questions.Title: Question 23
Questions.QuestionText: If events A and B are independent, then P(A|B) equals:
Questions.Feedback: If A and B are independent, then P(A|B) = P(A), meaning the occurrence of B does not affect the probability of A occurring

Questions.Title: Question 24
Questions.QuestionText: In a medical test, P(Positive|Disease) = 0.9, P(Positive|No Disease) = 0.1, and P(Disease) = 0.01. What is P(Positive)?
Questions.Feedback: P(Positive) = P(Positive|Disease)×P(Disease) + P(Positive|No Disease)×P(No Disease) = 0.9×0.01 + 0.1×0.99 = 0.009 + 0.099 = 0.109

Questions.Title: Question 25
Questions.QuestionText: In a standard 52-card deck, what is the probability of drawing a red card?
Questions.Feedback: In a 52-card deck, there are 26 red cards (hearts and diamonds), so the probability is 26/52 = 1/2

Questions.Title: Question 26
Questions.QuestionText: If P(A) = 0.7, P(B) = 0.6, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.4, what is P(A ∪ B)?

Questions.Title: Question 27
Questions.QuestionText: When rolling a fair six-sided die, what is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
Questions.Feedback: Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3

Questions.Title: Question 28
Questions.QuestionText: If the probability of rain tomorrow is 0.75, what is the probability it will not rain?
Questions.Feedback: The probability of no rain is P(no rain) = 1 - P(rain) = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25

Questions.Title: Question 29
Questions.QuestionText: In a factory, machine A produces 30% of items, and machine B produces 70%. Machine A has a 3% defect rate, while machine B has a 1% defect rate. If an item is defective, what is the probability it was produced by machine A?
Questions.Feedback: Using Bayes' theorem: P(A|defect) = [P(defect|A)×P(A)]/[P(defect|A)×P(A) + P(defect|B)×P(B)] = [0.03×0.3]/[0.03×0.3 + 0.01×0.7] = 0.009/0.016 = 0.563

Questions.QuestionText: If P(A) = 0.5 and P(B|A) = 0.4, what is P(A ∩ B)?

Questions.Title: Question 31
Questions.QuestionText: Two events with non-zero probabilities can be:
Questions.Feedback: Events with non-zero probabilities can be independent but not mutually exclusive. If they were mutually exclusive, P(A ∩ B) = 0, which contradicts the independence criterion P(A ∩ B) = P(A)×P(B) ≠ 0

Questions.Title: Question 32
Questions.QuestionText: If you flip a fair coin 4 times, what is the probability of getting at least one head?
Questions.Feedback: P(at least one head) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - P(all tails) = 1 - (1/2)^4 = 1 - 1/16 = 15/16 = 0.9375

Questions.Title: Question 33
Questions.QuestionText: If P(A|C) = P(A) and P(B|C) = P(B), then events A and B are:
Questions.Feedback: This is the definition of conditional independence given C, meaning that when C occurs, knowing about A doesn't change the probability of B and vice versa

Questions.Title: Question 34
Questions.QuestionText: In a Venn diagram of events A and B, the region where A and B overlap represents:
Questions.Feedback: The overlap region in a Venn diagram represents the intersection of the two events - outcomes that belong to both event A and event B, denoted P(A ∩ B)

Questions.Title: Question 35
Questions.QuestionText: Which statement is true about disjoint (mutually exclusive) events A and B?
Questions.Feedback: For mutually exclusive events, P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) = 0/P(B) = 0, assuming P(B) > 0

Questions.Title: Question 36
Questions.QuestionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the basic axioms of probability?
Questions.Feedback: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) is only true for mutually exclusive events. The general formula is P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)

Options.Text: P(Ω) = 1, where Ω is the sample space
For any two events A and B, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)
If A₁, A₂, ... are mutually exclusive events, then P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ ...) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + ...

Questions.Title: Question 37
Questions.QuestionText: What is the sample space for the experiment of rolling two fair dice and recording the sum?
Questions.Feedback: When rolling two dice and recording their sum, the possible outcomes are the integers from 2 to 12 inclusive

Questions.Title: Question 38
Questions.QuestionText: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. If the first ball drawn is red, what is the probability the second is also red?
Questions.Feedback: After drawing a red ball, 3 red and 6 blue balls remain. The probability of drawing another red is 3/(3+6) = 3/9 = 1/3

Questions.Title: Question 39
Questions.QuestionText: Given P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.12, are events A and B independent?
Questions.Feedback: Events A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Here, P(A) × P(B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12 = P(A ∩ B), so they are independent

Questions.Title: Question 40
Questions.QuestionText: From a standard 52-card deck, you draw 2 cards without replacement. What is the probability of drawing 2 aces?
Questions.Feedback: The probability of the first card being an ace is 4/52. After drawing an ace, there are 3 aces left among 51 cards, so the probability of the second card being an ace is 3/51. Therefore, P(2 aces) = (4/52) × (3/51) = 1/221

Questions.Title: Question 41
Questions.QuestionText: When rolling a fair six-sided die once, which is NOT an event?
Questions.Feedback: An event must be a subset of the sample space. Since the sample space for a six-sided die is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, getting a 7 is not a possible outcome and thus not an event

Questions.Title: Question 42
Questions.QuestionText: In how many ways can you select 3 cards from a standard 52-card deck?
Questions.Feedback: The number of ways to select 3 cards from 52 cards is C(52,3) = 52! / (3! × 49!) = 22,100

Questions.Title: Question 43
Questions.QuestionText: Which formula correctly defines P(A|B)?
Questions.Feedback: The conditional probability of A given B is defined as P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), where P(B) > 0

Questions.Title: Question 44
Questions.QuestionText: For any event A, which formula is always true?
Questions.Feedback: For any event A, P(A) + P(A') = 1, since an event either occurs or it doesn't, and these are mutually exclusive and exhaustive possibilities

Questions.Title: Question 45
Questions.QuestionText: In a room of 23 people, the probability that at least 2 people share a birthday is approximately:
Questions.Feedback: In the Birthday Problem, with 23 people the probability of at least one shared birthday is approximately 0.507 (slightly greater than 0.5), which is surprisingly high for many people
